locations.name: The Brooklyn Bridge
locations.factShort: Its designer died of tetanus before construction began, and his son took over only to be crippled by decompression sickness in the caissons. His wife Emily then ran the project for eleven years, learning the engineering as she went, and rode across first with a rooster in her lap.

locations.name: Grand Central Terminal
locations.factShort: The ceiling's zodiac is painted backwards, which the Vanderbilts explained away as the view from God's perspective; it was more likely a plasterer working from a reversed medieval drawing. The building was saved from demolition in 1978 by a Supreme Court case Jackie Onassis helped fight.

locations.name: The Unisphere
locations.factShort: Built for the 1964 World's Fair by U.S. Steel, the twelve-storey globe was meant to be dismantled afterwards and never was. Three rings around it mark the orbits of the first satellites, put there when spaceflight was six years old.

locations.name: Green-Wood Cemetery
locations.factShort: In the 1850s it drew half a million visitors a year, second only to Niagara Falls, and its popularity as a place to simply walk is what convinced the city it needed Central Park. Its highest point was where Washington watched the Battle of Long Island go badly wrong.

locations.name: The Alice Austen House
locations.query: Alice Austen House, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: Alice Austen made some 8,000 photographs of New York from the 1880s onward, then lost everything in the 1929 crash and died in a poorhouse. A historian found her negatives in a Staten Island archive in 1951 and got her moved to a nursing home months before she died.

locations.name: Times Square
locations.factShort: It was Longacre Square until The New York Times moved in and got the subway station renamed in 1904. The paper left in 1913 but kept dropping the New Year's ball from the old building, which is why the countdown happens where it does.

locations.name: Prospect Park
locations.factShort: Olmsted and Vaux considered it better than Central Park, which they had finished a few years earlier, because here they were not fighting an awkward rectangle. It holds Brooklyn's last remaining tract of old-growth forest.

locations.name: The Bronx Zoo
locations.factShort: It saved the American bison from extinction, breeding a herd in the Bronx and shipping animals west to restock the plains. It also, disgracefully, exhibited a Congolese man named Ota Benga in the monkey house in 1906.

locations.name: The Cloisters
locations.factShort: Rockefeller bought up medieval French cloisters, had them shipped stone by stone and reassembled into one building that never existed in Europe. He also bought the New Jersey palisades opposite so nothing would ever spoil the view from it.

locations.name: The Bowne House
locations.factShort: John Bowne let Quakers meet in his kitchen in 1662, was arrested and shipped to Amsterdam, and argued his way to an acquittal that forced New Netherland to tolerate them. The house still stands, and the argument is treated as an ancestor of the First Amendment.

locations.name: The Statue of Liberty
locations.factShort: The arm and torch were exhibited in Madison Square for six years to raise money for a pedestal New York was reluctant to pay for. Joseph Pulitzer eventually shamed the city into it by printing the name of every small donor in his newspaper.

locations.name: The Cyclone
locations.factShort: The wooden coaster has run since 1927 on a first drop of eighty-five feet at a slope steeper than most modern steel rides manage. Charles Lindbergh reportedly said riding it was more frightening than flying the Atlantic.

locations.name: The New York Botanical Garden
locations.factShort: Fifty acres of it are old-growth forest that has never been logged, the last uncut remnant of the woodland that covered the whole city. Its herbarium holds around eight million preserved plant specimens.

locations.name: The Stonewall Inn
locations.factShort: It was a mafia-run bar without running water behind the counter, which is partly why it was raided so often. The June 1969 raid met resistance instead of compliance, and the bar became the first LGBTQ site named a national monument.

locations.name: Weeksville Heritage Center
locations.factShort: James Weeks, a free Black longshoreman, bought land here in 1838 and built one of the largest free Black communities in pre-Civil War America, with its own school, church and newspaper. It was forgotten entirely until a 1968 flight over Brooklyn spotted four surviving houses on a forgotten lane.

locations.name: The Flatiron Building
locations.factShort: Its wedge shape funnelled wind down Fifth Avenue hard enough to lift women's skirts, drawing loiterers whom police shooed away — reportedly the origin of the phrase twenty-three skidoo. Critics expected it to topple and nicknamed it Burnham's Folly.

locations.name: The Brooklyn Museum
locations.factShort: McKim, Mead and White designed it to be four times its built size, as the centrepiece of an independent City of Brooklyn that was absorbed into New York before the plan could finish. Its Egyptian collection is among the best anywhere outside Cairo and London.

locations.name: Citi Field
locations.factShort: Its brick facade and rotunda copy Ebbets Field, home of a Brooklyn team that left for Los Angeles in 1957 — an odd tribute for a Queens ballpark to a stadium demolished in 1960. It replaced Shea Stadium, whose outline is marked in the car park next door.

locations.name: Woodlawn Cemetery
locations.factShort: Duke Ellington, Miles Davis, Celia Cruz and Max Roach are all buried within a few hundred yards of each other, making it something close to a jazz pantheon. Its mausoleums were commissioned from the same architects who built the Gilded Age mansions their owners lived in.

locations.name: The Conference House
locations.query: Conference House, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: In September 1776 Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge met Admiral Howe here in the only peace conference of the Revolutionary War. It lasted three hours, failed over the question of independence, and the war ran another seven years.

locations.name: The Chrysler Building
locations.factShort: Its architect kept a 125-foot spire hidden inside the building and raised it in ninety minutes to beat a rival tower downtown, holding the world's-tallest title for eleven months before the Empire State opened. The eagles at the corners are modelled on Chrysler hood ornaments.

locations.name: The Brooklyn Heights Promenade
locations.factShort: Robert Moses wanted an expressway through Brooklyn Heights; residents fought him to a compromise where the road runs beneath a cantilevered public walkway. The neighbourhood got the view, and the traffic runs invisibly under their feet.

locations.name: Rockaway Beach
locations.factShort: It is the largest urban beach in the United States and the only legal surfing beach in the city, reachable by subway. Sandy destroyed much of the boardwalk in 2012, and the rebuilt one doubles as a sea wall.

locations.name: The Edgar Allan Poe Cottage
locations.factShort: Poe moved his dying wife here in 1846 hoping country air would help; she died that winter under his old army coat, and he wrote Annabel Lee and The Bells in the rooms that remain. The farmland around it is now the Grand Concourse.

locations.name: Kingsland Homestead
locations.factShort: The house has been moved twice to escape demolition, most recently in 1968, and now sits beside the stump of a weeping beech that was a landmark in its own right. Its Quaker owner freed his slaves decades before New York required it.

locations.name: The Washington Square Arch
locations.factShort: A temporary plaster arch put up for Washington's inaugural centenary proved so popular it was rebuilt in marble. In 1917 a group of artists picnicked on top and declared Greenwich Village a free and independent republic.

locations.name: Barclays Center
locations.factShort: Its rusted steel skin is deliberate — weathering steel that corrodes into a protective layer and then stops. Building it required one of the most contested uses of eminent domain in modern New York.

locations.name: The Museum of the Moving Image
locations.prompt: The Museum of the Moving Image
locations.query: Museum of the Moving Image, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: It occupies part of Kaufman Astoria Studios, where Paramount made films before the industry left for California. The Marx Brothers and W. C. Fields worked on the lot; Sesame Street still does.

locations.name: Wave Hill
locations.factShort: Mark Twain rented the house one winter and built a treehouse in the grounds; Toscanini and Theodore Roosevelt's family also lived here at different times. The city took it over in 1960 and turned twenty-eight acres above the Hudson into a public garden.

locations.name: Historic Richmond Town
locations.query: Historic Richmond Town, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: Thirty buildings across a hundred acres, including the Voorlezer's House of about 1695 — the oldest surviving schoolhouse in the country. Some were built here; others were moved in from around the island to save them.

locations.name: The High Line
locations.factShort: It was a freight viaduct built to lift trains off Tenth Avenue, where they had killed so many people the street was called Death Avenue. Abandoned in 1980, it was days from demolition when two neighbours who liked the self-seeded weeds on it started a campaign.

locations.name: Nathan's Famous
locations.factShort: Nathan Handwerker undercut his former employer by charging five cents instead of ten, then hired men in surgeons' coats to eat at the counter so the cheap price would not look suspect. The original stand is still on the corner of Surf and Stillwell.

locations.name: The Queens Museum
locations.factShort: It holds the Panorama of the City of New York, a 9,335-square-foot scale model of all five boroughs with every building standing in 1992. The building itself housed the United Nations General Assembly from 1946 to 1950.

locations.name: McSorley's Old Ale House
locations.query: McSorley's Old Ale House, New York
locations.factShort: It serves two things, light ale and dark ale, always two mugs at a time, and the wishbones hanging over the bar were left by men going to the First World War who never came back to collect them. It refused to admit women until a 1970 lawsuit forced it.

locations.name: The Van Cortlandt House
locations.query: Van Cortlandt House Museum, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: The oldest building in the Bronx, and the place Washington used as a headquarters more than once — he lit decoy campfires here to cover his march to Yorktown. City records were hidden in a vault on the grounds during the Revolution.

locations.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral
locations.factShort: When begun in 1858 it stood well outside the built city and was mocked as Hughes's Folly, a cathedral in a cow pasture. Construction paused for the Civil War and the spires were not finished until 1888.

locations.name: Grand Army Plaza
locations.query: Grand Army Plaza, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: The Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial Arch honours the Union dead, and its interior once held bronze reliefs of Lincoln and Grant by a young sculptor named Frederick MacMonnies. Olmsted and Vaux designed the oval as a formal entrance to Prospect Park.

locations.name: The Noguchi Museum
locations.factShort: Isamu Noguchi bought a photo-engraving plant across from his studio and converted it himself, designing every gallery around his own work. He was interned at Poston during the war, having volunteered to enter the camp.

locations.name: The Morris-Jumel Mansion
locations.factShort: Manhattan's oldest surviving house, and Washington's headquarters in the autumn of 1776. Later Eliza Jumel, one of the richest women in America, lived here and briefly married Aaron Burr; she divorced him on the day he died.

locations.name: The Wyckoff House
locations.query: Wyckoff House Museum, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Parts of it date to about 1652, making it the oldest building in New York City and the first structure the city ever designated a landmark. It survived because the Wyckoff family held the farm for eight generations.

locations.name: Rockefeller Center
locations.factShort: It was conceived as a new opera house; the crash killed that plan and left Rockefeller with a lease he could not escape, so he built an office complex instead. Diego Rivera's mural was destroyed for including Lenin.

locations.name: The Gowanus Canal
locations.factShort: A century and a half of gasworks, tanneries and raw sewage made it one of the most contaminated waterways in the country, declared a Superfund site in 2010. The black sludge on its bed is known locally as black mayonnaise.

locations.name: City Island
locations.factShort: A mile-and-a-half island in the Bronx that reads as a New England fishing town, reached by one bridge. Its boatyards built America's Cup defenders, and residents born there call themselves clam diggers.

locations.name: The Village Vanguard
locations.factShort: A wedge-shaped basement of about 120 seats where Coltrane, Evans and Rollins all made records that are still in print. It opened in 1935 for poetry and folk and only turned fully to jazz in the fifties.

locations.name: Snug Harbor
locations.factShort: Built as a retirement home for aged sailors under a bequest that the courts fought over for years, it grew to fifty buildings and nearly a thousand residents. The Greek Revival row facing the water is among the finest in the country.

locations.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
locations.query: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
locations.factShort: It was founded in a Paris restaurant in 1866 by Americans who thought their country needed a national gallery, and opened with not a single object in its collection. Admission was a suggested donation for decades, an arrangement that ended in 2018 for out-of-state visitors.

locations.name: The Parachute Jump
locations.factShort: Built for the 1939 World's Fair in Queens and moved to Coney Island in 1941, it dropped riders 250 feet under real parachutes until it closed in 1968. It has been lit but not operational for over fifty years, and is called Brooklyn's Eiffel Tower.

locations.name: The Hell Gate Bridge
locations.factShort: When it opened in 1916 it was the longest steel arch in the world, and it was built so massively that engineers estimate it would be the last New York bridge standing if people vanished. Sydney Harbour Bridge is a direct descendant of its design.

locations.name: Arthur Avenue
locations.factShort: The Bronx's Little Italy, and a strong claim to being a more intact one than Manhattan's. The covered retail market was built in 1940 because Fiorello La Guardia wanted the pushcarts off the street.

locations.name: The Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge
locations.query: Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: Over 300 bird species have been recorded in a federal wildlife refuge that sits under the approach path to JFK and is reachable by subway. The two freshwater ponds at its heart are entirely artificial, dug in the 1950s by a parks employee on his own initiative.

locations.name: The Guggenheim Museum
locations.query: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
locations.factShort: Wright spent sixteen years on it and died six months before it opened. Twenty-one artists signed a letter protesting that the sloping spiral walls were a hostile place to hang a painting.

locations.name: Gantry Plaza State Park
locations.query: Gantry Plaza State Park, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: The two black gantries were used to lift rail carriages on and off barges crossing the East River, back when no tunnel carried freight into Manhattan. They were kept as sculpture when the rail yard became a park.

locations.name: Hamilton Grange
locations.query: Hamilton Grange National Memorial, New York
locations.factShort: Alexander Hamilton's only owned home, finished two years before Burr killed him. It has been moved twice, most recently in 2008, when it was lifted over a church and rolled into St. Nicholas Park.

locations.name: Fort Totten
locations.factShort: A Civil War fort begun in 1862 to guard the eastern approach to New York, made obsolete before completion by rifled artillery that its granite could not withstand. Robert E. Lee surveyed the site years before the war he would fight on the other side of.

locations.name: The Bartow-Pell Mansion
locations.factShort: A Greek Revival house on land the Pell family bought from the Siwanoy in 1654, in what is now the city's largest park. Fiorello La Guardia used it as a summer City Hall.

locations.name: The 9/11 Memorial
locations.factShort: The two pools sit exactly in the footprints of the towers, and the names around them are arranged by what the designers called meaningful adjacency — colleagues, friends and those who died together, placed together at families' request. One pear tree that survived the collapse was nursed back and replanted.

locations.name: Fort Greene Park
locations.query: Fort Greene Park, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Beneath its central monument lie the remains of some 11,500 people who died on British prison ships in Wallabout Bay — more American deaths than in all the war's battles combined. Walt Whitman campaigned for the park while editing the Brooklyn Eagle.

locations.name: Socrates Sculpture Park
locations.query: Socrates Sculpture Park, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: An illegal dumping ground on the East River until the sculptor Mark di Suvero and local artists cleared it themselves in 1986 and started showing work on it. The city only made it an official park in 1998.

locations.name: Grant's Tomb
locations.factShort: The largest mausoleum in North America, paid for by ninety thousand small donations after Grant asked to be buried where his wife could join him. Its dedication in 1897 drew a million people.

locations.name: Fort Wadsworth
locations.query: Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: Fortified continuously from the 1660s until 1994, which makes it one of the longest continuously garrisoned military sites in the country. The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge now springs directly over it.

locations.name: Lincoln Center
locations.factShort: Building it cleared the San Juan Hill neighbourhood, a largely Black and Puerto Rican district of some seven thousand families — the same blocks filmed for West Side Story shortly before demolition. Robert Moses called it slum clearance.

locations.name: The Apollo Theater
locations.factShort: It opened as a whites-only burlesque house and did not admit Black audiences until 1934, after which Amateur Night launched Ella Fitzgerald at seventeen, then Billie Holiday, James Brown and the Jackson 5. Performers still touch a stump of elm from the Tree of Hope for luck.

locations.name: Brighton Beach
locations.factShort: Named after the English resort and developed as a seaside escape in the 1860s, it became home to so many Soviet emigrants from the 1970s that it is widely called Little Odessa. The elevated train runs directly above the main street.

locations.name: The Flushing Quaker Meeting House
locations.factShort: Built in 1694 and in near-continuous use since, which makes it the oldest place of worship in the city. Its congregation produced the Flushing Remonstrance of 1657, a petition for religious tolerance written a century before the Constitution.

locations.name: The Chinese Scholar's Garden
locations.factShort: One of only two authentic classical Chinese gardens in the United States, built by forty artisans from Suzhou who assembled it on site from components shipped over. It sits inside the grounds of a nineteenth-century sailors' retirement home.

locations.name: The New York Public Library
locations.factShort: It stands on the drained bed of the Croton Reservoir, whose Egyptian-style walls held the city's water supply until 1900. The lions were named Patience and Fortitude by La Guardia during the Depression, for the qualities he thought New Yorkers needed.

locations.name: Kings Theatre
locations.factShort: A 1929 Loew's Wonder Theatre that sat derelict for thirty-eight years with rain coming through the roof onto its plasterwork. A ninety-five million dollar restoration reopened it in 2015, matching the original French Baroque interior from photographs.

locations.name: The Steinway & Sons Factory
locations.factShort: Steinway built not just a factory here but a company town with housing, a school and a fire station, on farmland far from Manhattan's labour unrest. Each concert grand still takes about a year to build, much of it by hand.

locations.name: The Grand Concourse
locations.factShort: Modelled on the Champs-Élysées and opened in 1909, its four-and-a-half miles hold one of the largest concentrations of Art Deco apartment buildings anywhere. It was cut through farmland years before the subway that would fill it arrived.

locations.name: The Lemon Ice King of Corona
locations.prompt: The Lemon Ice King of Corona
locations.query: Lemon Ice King of Corona, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: Selling Italian ices on the same corner since 1944, in around thirty flavours, and famously refusing to put them in a cup with ice cream. The corner park outside appears in the opening credits of King of Queens.

locations.name: The Roosevelt Island Tramway
locations.factShort: Built in 1976 as a stopgap until the subway reached the island, and kept because people liked it — the first commuter aerial tram in North America. It runs on a MetroCard swipe.

locations.name: The Brooklyn Botanic Garden
locations.factShort: Built on a former ash dump beside Prospect Park, it opened in 1911 with the first Japanese garden created for an American public park. Its cherry esplanade draws crowds each spring that rival the Washington tidal basin.

locations.name: Orchard Beach
locations.factShort: Robert Moses joined two islands to the mainland with landfill and barged in sand from Queens and New Jersey to build the Bronx its only public beach. Locals call it the Bronx Riviera.

locations.name: The Chelsea Hotel
locations.factShort: Dylan Thomas drank himself to death from here, Arthur C. Clarke wrote 2001 in it, and Leonard Cohen wrote a song about a night in one of its rooms. It was the tallest building in New York when it opened in 1884.

locations.name: The Queens Giant
locations.query: Alley Pond Park, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: A tulip tree in Alley Pond Park estimated at 350 to 450 years old, the oldest living thing in New York City — already standing when the Dutch arrived. Its location is kept vague to protect it.

locations.name: Bryant Park
locations.factShort: By the 1970s it was so given over to drug dealing that people called it Needle Park, and it was closed and redesigned in 1988 using William Whyte's studies of how people actually use public space. Its moveable chairs were a deliberate part of that.

locations.name: The Brooklyn Navy Yard
locations.factShort: It built the Monitor's rival ships, the Maine, the Arizona and the Missouri, on whose deck Japan surrendered. Seventy thousand people worked here during the Second World War, a third of them women.

locations.name: Jackson Heights
locations.factShort: One of America's first planned garden-apartment communities, built around private interior gardens in the 1910s. It is now among the most linguistically diverse places on earth, with more than 160 languages spoken in the district.

locations.name: The Woolworth Building
locations.factShort: Frank Woolworth paid 13.5 million dollars for it in cash, out of nickel-and-dime store profits, and it was the tallest building in the world until 1930. A clergyman called it the Cathedral of Commerce and the name stuck.

locations.name: Sunnyside Gardens
locations.factShort: A 1920s experiment in affordable housing built around shared interior courtyards, with Lewis Mumford among its first residents and its planners. It was designed to be walkable and low-rise at a time when the city was building tenements.

locations.name: Union Square
locations.factShort: Named not for the Union but for the union of two roads, it has been the city's default protest ground since the first American Labor Day march passed through in 1882. After 9/11 it became a spontaneous shrine of candles and notes.

locations.name: Peter Luger Steak House
locations.query: Peter Luger Steak House, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Open since 1887 under the Williamsburg Bridge, it grades and dry-ages its own beef and for most of its history took no credit cards at all. There is effectively one thing on the menu and the waiters will tell you so.

locations.name: Fort Tilden
locations.factShort: A coastal battery that ended its life holding Nike missiles aimed at Soviet bombers, now a beach where concrete bunkers sit in the dunes. It has no lifeguards and a long walk from the road, which is why it stays quiet.

locations.name: The Cooper Union
locations.factShort: Peter Cooper, who had almost no schooling himself, founded it in 1859 to be free and open to all regardless of race or sex. Lincoln's speech in its Great Hall in 1860 is widely credited with making him president.

locations.name: The St. George Ferry Terminal
locations.query: St. George Terminal, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: The Staten Island Ferry carries around twenty million passengers a year and has been free since 1997, making it the busiest free ferry route in the world. The terminal burned down in 1946 and was rebuilt, then rebuilt again in 2005.

locations.name: The American Museum of Natural History
locations.prompt: The American Museum of Natural History
locations.query: American Museum of Natural History, New York
locations.factShort: Its blue whale hangs from the ceiling at ninety-four feet, modelled in 1969 from a carcass photographed off South America because nobody had measured a living one. The dinosaur halls hold the largest fossil collection anywhere.

locations.name: The Williamsburg Bridge
locations.factShort: When it opened in 1903 it took the longest-suspension-span title from the Brooklyn Bridge, and it was built cheap and steel-heavy rather than beautiful. It carried so many Lower East Side families across that it was nicknamed the Jews' Highway.

locations.name: The Ridgewood Reservoir
locations.factShort: Drained in 1989 after a century supplying Brooklyn with water, its three empty basins were left alone and grew into genuine forest and wetland inside the city. Birders now record over 130 species in it.

locations.name: The High Bridge
locations.factShort: The oldest surviving bridge in New York, built in 1848 to carry Croton water into Manhattan on Roman-style stone arches. Closed for over forty years, it reopened as a footbridge in 2015.

locations.name: The Garibaldi-Meucci Museum
locations.query: Garibaldi-Meucci Museum, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: Antonio Meucci, who demonstrated a working telephone years before Bell's patent, sheltered Giuseppe Garibaldi here between Italian revolutions. Garibaldi worked in Meucci's candle factory while waiting to go back and unify Italy.

locations.name: Carnegie Hall
locations.factShort: Tchaikovsky conducted at its opening in 1891. It was nearly demolished for an office tower in 1960 until the violinist Isaac Stern led a campaign that got the city to buy it.

locations.name: Jane's Carousel
locations.factShort: A 1922 Ohio carousel bought at auction and restored horse by horse over twenty-odd years by the woman it is named for. Its glass pavilion sat in floodwater during Sandy with the carousel dry inside.

locations.name: King Manor
locations.factShort: Rufus King signed the Constitution, was one of the first senators from New York, and argued against slavery's extension from this farmhouse. His son later became governor of the state.

locations.name: The Hunts Point Market
locations.query: Hunts Point Cooperative Market, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: The largest food distribution centre in the world by some measures, moving several billion dollars of produce, meat and fish a year across three hundred acres. Most of what New York eats passes through here overnight.

locations.name: Floyd Bennett Field
locations.query: Floyd Bennett Field, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: New York's first municipal airport, which failed commercially because it was too far from Manhattan, then became a record-setting field — Howard Hughes and Wiley Post both flew from it. Its runways are now cracked and grassed over inside a national park.

locations.name: Radio City Music Hall
locations.query: Radio City Music Hall, New York
locations.factShort: The largest indoor theatre in the world when it opened in 1932, with a stage designed to look like a setting sun and hydraulics borrowed from aircraft-carrier lifts. It nearly closed in 1978 before landmark status saved it.

locations.name: The Brooklyn Academy of Music
locations.factShort: America's oldest continuously operating performing arts centre, founded in 1861. Its original building burned down in 1903; the replacement opened with Caruso singing Faust.

locations.name: The New York Hall of Science
locations.prompt: The New York Hall of Science
locations.query: New York Hall of Science, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: Built for the 1964 World's Fair and one of the few pavilions kept, its Great Hall is a curving wall of cobalt-blue glass set in concrete. It was left derelict through the 1970s before reopening as a science museum.

locations.name: The Morris High School Historic District
locations.prompt: The Morris High School Historic District
locations.query: Morris High School, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: The Bronx's first public high school, opened in 1904, with an auditorium of stained glass and carved oak that is a city landmark in its own right. Colin Powell graduated from it.

locations.name: The Moravian Cemetery
locations.query: Moravian Cemetery, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: The oldest cemetery on Staten Island, holding a Vanderbilt mausoleum that Richard Morris Hunt designed and Frederick Law Olmsted landscaped. Cornelius Vanderbilt was born a few miles away and is buried in it.

locations.name: The Battery
locations.factShort: Named for the gun batteries that once faced the harbour, and the point from which most of Manhattan's later shoreline was landfilled outward. Castle Clinton inside it processed eight million immigrants before Ellis Island opened.

locations.name: Valentino Pier
locations.factShort: A short pier in Red Hook with one of the only street-level views of the Statue of Liberty from land. It is named for a firefighter who died in a Brooklyn blaze in 1996.

locations.name: The Queens County Farm Museum
locations.query: Queens County Farm Museum, New York
locations.factShort: Farmed continuously since 1697, which makes it the longest continuously farmed site in New York State, on forty-seven acres inside the city. It keeps livestock and grows a maze of corn each autumn.

locations.name: The Kingsbridge Armory
locations.factShort: Its drill hall is one of the largest unobstructed interior spaces in the world, big enough to hold a full city block. Empty since 1996, it has outlasted two decades of redevelopment plans.

locations.name: The Eldridge Street Synagogue
locations.query: Museum at Eldridge Street, New York
locations.factShort: The first great synagogue built in America by Eastern European Jews, opened in 1887 and grand enough to seat a thousand. Its congregation shrank so far that the main sanctuary was sealed off for decades and only reopened after a twenty-year restoration.

locations.name: The Cathedral of St. John the Divine
locations.prompt: The Cathedral of St. John the Divine
locations.query: Cathedral of St. John the Divine, New York
locations.factShort: Begun in 1892 and still unfinished, which has earned it the nickname St. John the Unfinished. It is among the largest church buildings in the world and its stonework halted for decades at a time.

locations.name: The Riegelmann Boardwalk
locations.factShort: Two and a half miles of boardwalk opened in 1923, built after the city seized the beachfront from private owners who had been charging for access. Most of its planks are now recycled plastic rather than tropical hardwood.

locations.name: MoMA PS1
locations.factShort: A derelict Victorian public school taken over by artists in 1976 as one of the first institutions anywhere devoted to installation work made on site. James Turrell cut a hole in its roof that frames nothing but sky.

locations.name: Crotona Park
locations.factShort: Its lake is a natural glacial kettle pond, and the park holds over two dozen tree species on land the Bathgate family sold to the city under protest. Its pool was one of eleven Robert Moses opened in a single Depression summer.

locations.name: Wolfe's Pond Park
locations.query: Wolfe's Pond Park, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: A freshwater pond separated from Raritan Bay by nothing but a sand bar, on land once owned by an oysterman named Wolfe. Its woods are among the quietest in the city.

locations.name: Madison Square Garden
locations.factShort: The current building is the fourth of its name and none of the last three stood on Madison Square. Building it required demolishing the original Penn Station in 1963, an act of vandalism that created the modern preservation movement.

locations.name: The Prospect Park Boathouse
locations.factShort: Modelled on a Venetian library and finished in 1905, it was scheduled for demolition in 1964 until a public campaign saved it. It now houses the country's first urban Audubon centre.

locations.name: The Marine Air Terminal
locations.factShort: Built in 1940 for the transatlantic flying boats that took off from the water beside it, and the only active terminal in the world still serving from that era. A mural inside was painted over during the McCarthy years and restored in the 1980s.

locations.name: Fordham University Rose Hill
locations.factShort: Founded in 1841 on a farm, its Gothic quadrangle is old enough that Edgar Allan Poe walked over from his cottage to ring the bells. The campus has stood in for Cambridge and Oxford in more than one film.

locations.name: The Dyckman Farmhouse
locations.factShort: The only Dutch colonial farmhouse left in Manhattan, built about 1785 on a farm that once ran to three hundred acres. Two Dyckman sisters bought it back in 1915 to stop it being demolished and gave it to the city.

locations.name: Washington Square Park
locations.factShort: It was a potter's field before it was a park, and an estimated twenty thousand people are still buried beneath it — bones surface whenever the city digs. Jane Jacobs stopped Robert Moses running a road through the middle of it.

locations.name: Sunset Park
locations.factShort: The hill gives one of the best free views in the city, taking in the harbour, both bridges and the Manhattan skyline at once. Its pool is a Robert Moses original from 1936.

locations.name: The Voelker Orth Museum
locations.factShort: A Victorian house kept by three generations of one family and left to the public as a museum, garden and bird sanctuary. Its owner published a German-language newspaper from Flushing.

locations.name: The Bronx Museum of the Arts
locations.prompt: The Bronx Museum of the Arts
locations.query: Bronx Museum of the Arts, New York
locations.factShort: Founded in 1971 in a synagogue on the Grand Concourse, it has been free to enter since 2012 and collects work by artists of African, Asian and Latin American descent. Its folded aluminium facade opened in 2006.

locations.name: Sandy Ground
locations.query: Sandy Ground, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: One of the oldest continuously settled free Black communities in the United States, founded in the 1830s by oystermen from Maryland who came north where they could own their boats. Descendants of the founding families still live there.

locations.name: Washington Street, Dumbo
locations.query: Washington Street, Dumbo, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: The single most photographed street corner in Brooklyn, where the Manhattan Bridge is framed exactly between two warehouse walls. The neighbourhood's name was invented by residents in the 1970s to sound ugly enough to deter developers.

locations.name: The Strand
locations.factShort: The last survivor of Fourth Avenue's Book Row, which held some forty-eight bookshops in the 1940s. It advertises eighteen miles of books, a figure it has since revised upward.

locations.name: The Forest Park Carousel
locations.query: Forest Park Carousel, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: It carries some of the last surviving horses carved by Daniel Muller, widely held to be the finest carousel carver who ever worked in America. It is one of very few carousels to be designated a landmark for the animals rather than the building.

locations.name: St. Ann's Church
locations.query: St. Ann's Church, Mott Haven, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: The oldest church building in the Bronx, built in 1841 by Gouverneur Morris II as a memorial to his mother. Her father Lewis Morris, a signer of the Declaration, is buried in the vault beneath.

locations.name: Chumley's
locations.factShort: A Prohibition speakeasy with no sign and two exits, one onto a courtyard — the back way out is a common explanation for the phrase eighty-six it. Its ceiling collapsed in 2007 and it took nearly a decade to reopen.

locations.name: Columbus Circle
locations.factShort: Every distance from New York City is officially measured from this point. The Columbus monument was funded by Italian-Americans through a newspaper appeal after the city declined to pay.

locations.name: Industry City
locations.factShort: Sixteen buildings built as Bush Terminal, once the largest multi-tenant industrial complex in the country, with its own rail and shipping piers. It employed twenty-five thousand people at its peak.

locations.name: The Court Square Clock Tower
locations.query: Bank of Manhattan Company Building, Long Island City, Queens
locations.factShort: For sixty years this was the tallest building in Queens and the only tower on the skyline east of the river. Its four clock faces were dark for decades before being relit.

locations.name: Concrete Plant Park
locations.factShort: A derelict concrete batching plant on the Bronx River, whose rusted hoppers and conveyor frames were kept and painted as the centrepiece of a park. The river beside it was called an open sewer in the 1970s; beavers returned to it in 2007, the first seen in New York in two hundred years.

locations.name: Todt Hill
locations.query: Todt Hill, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: At about 401 feet it is the highest natural point on the eastern seaboard south of Maine. Its bedrock is serpentine, a greenish rock rare enough in the region to be a geological curiosity.

locations.name: The Plaza Hotel
locations.factShort: It opened in 1907 and Alfred Vanderbilt was the first guest to sign the register. Eloise, the fictional six-year-old who lives on the top floor, has her portrait hanging in the lobby.

locations.name: The Lefferts Historic House
locations.factShort: A Dutch farmhouse rebuilt in the 1780s after the original was burned during the Battle of Long Island. It was moved into Prospect Park in 1918 when the family gave it to the city.

locations.name: Silvercup Studios
locations.factShort: A former bread bakery whose rooftop sign is still lit, converted in 1983 into the largest film studio in the northeast. The Sopranos, Sex and the City and Highlander were all shot inside it.

locations.name: The Andrew Freedman Home
locations.query: Andrew Freedman Home, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: A subway contractor left his fortune to build a mansion where people who had been wealthy and lost it could live out their lives in the style they were used to, with servants and black-tie dinners. The last resident left in the 1980s.

locations.name: The Merchant's House Museum
locations.factShort: The only nineteenth-century family home in New York preserved intact inside and out, down to the Tredwell family's furniture and clothing. One daughter lived in it for ninety-three years and changed almost nothing.

locations.name: The Charging Bull
locations.factShort: Arturo Di Modica made it at his own expense and dumped it outside the Stock Exchange one night in December 1989 without permission. The city removed it within hours, then put it back two blocks away after public protest.

locations.name: Erasmus Hall
locations.query: Erasmus Hall High School, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Founded in 1786 as the first secondary school chartered in New York State, with Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr both among its early donors. Barbra Streisand and Neil Diamond were in its choir at the same time.

locations.name: Maple Grove Cemetery
locations.factShort: Opened in 1875 with its own railway station so mourners could arrive by train from Manhattan. The neighbourhood of Kew Gardens grew up around it afterwards.

locations.name: The Hall of Fame for Great Americans
locations.prompt: The Hall of Fame for Great Americans
locations.query: Hall of Fame for Great Americans, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: America's first hall of fame, a 630-foot open-air colonnade by Stanford White holding bronze busts elected by a national vote. Nobody has been added since 1976.

locations.name: The National Lighthouse Museum
locations.query: National Lighthouse Museum, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: Built as the Lighthouse Service's national depot, where every lens and lamp in American waters was tested and maintained. The site supplied lighthouses from Maine to the Gulf for nearly a century.

locations.name: The Grand Central Oyster Bar
locations.query: Grand Central Oyster Bar, New York
locations.factShort: It opened with the terminal in 1913 beneath Guastavino tile vaults, and the whispering gallery outside carries a murmur clean across the arch. It went bankrupt in 1972 and was revived by a Long Island restaurateur.

locations.name: Gravesend Cemetery
locations.factShort: Gravesend was chartered in 1645 under Lady Deborah Moody, the only colonial American settlement founded by a woman. Its original sixteen-square street plan is still legible in the blocks around the graveyard.

locations.name: The Poppenhusen Institute
locations.factShort: A rubber manufacturer built it in 1868 as a free school for his workers, and it housed the first free kindergarten in the United States. It also served as the local courthouse and jail.

locations.name: Fort Schuyler
locations.factShort: A granite fort finished in 1856 to cover the eastern approach to New York, never fired on in anger, and now the campus of a maritime college. Its walls are up to eight feet thick.

locations.name: The Bialystoker Synagogue
locations.factShort: Built in 1826 as a Methodist church from fieldstone quarried on the block, and bought by immigrants from Bialystok in 1905. A hidden attic above the women's balcony is said to have sheltered people on the Underground Railroad.

locations.name: Bethesda Terrace
locations.factShort: Its Angel of the Waters was the first major public art commission in New York given to a woman, Emma Stebbins, and celebrates the Croton Aqueduct bringing clean water to the city. The arcade ceiling holds nearly sixteen thousand encaustic tiles made in England.

locations.name: Brooklyn Bridge Park
locations.factShort: Eighty-five acres built on derelict shipping piers, with hills raised specifically to block expressway noise. Its salt marsh is the first tidal wetland restored in the East River in over a century.

locations.name: The Astoria Park Pool
locations.factShort: The largest and oldest of the eleven pools Robert Moses opened in the summer of 1936, big enough to hold three thousand swimmers. American Olympic trials were held in it in 1936 and 1964.

locations.name: Van Cortlandt Park
locations.query: Van Cortlandt Park, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: The city's third largest park, holding its largest freshwater marsh and the oldest golf course in the country. The Van Cortlandt family's grinding mill dammed the creek that made the lake.

locations.name: The Jacques Marchais Museum of Tibetan Art
locations.prompt: The Jacques Marchais Museum of Tibetan Art
locations.query: Jacques Marchais Museum of Tibetan Art, Staten Island
locations.factShort: Built in 1945 to resemble a Himalayan monastery by a woman who collected Tibetan art for decades and never once travelled to Asia. The Dalai Lama visited in 1991.

locations.name: The Vessel
locations.factShort: A climbable lattice of 154 interconnecting flights, some 2,500 steps that lead nowhere in particular. It closed for over a year after a series of deaths and reopened with floor-to-ceiling netting.

locations.name: L&B Spumoni Gardens
locations.query: L&B Spumoni Gardens, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Selling Sicilian squares with the cheese under the sauce since 1939, from a cart that became a restaurant. The spumoni is made on the premises to the founder's recipe.

locations.name: The Queens Botanical Garden
locations.factShort: It began as a five-acre exhibit at the 1939 World's Fair called Gardens on Parade and was kept when the fair closed. Its visitor centre was the first building in the city to earn a platinum green rating.

locations.name: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue
locations.factShort: DJ Kool Herc threw a back-to-school party in this building's recreation room on 11 August 1973, extending the breaks between records so dancers could keep going. It is widely treated as the birthplace of hip-hop.

locations.name: St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery
locations.factShort: The second oldest church building in Manhattan, standing on Peter Stuyvesant's farm chapel site with the man himself buried in the vault. It has hosted avant-garde poetry and dance since the 1960s.

locations.name: The Central Park Zoo
locations.factShort: It grew from a stray menagerie of donated animals dumped at the Arsenal in the 1860s, making it the second oldest public zoo in the country. Its 1930s cages were replaced entirely in 1988.

locations.name: Fort Hamilton
locations.factShort: An active army post since 1831, guarding the Narrows opposite Fort Wadsworth. Robert E. Lee served here as an engineer, and Stonewall Jackson was baptised in the chapel.

locations.name: Flushing Town Hall
locations.query: Flushing Town Hall, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: Built in 1862 and used for everything from courtroom to jail to opera house — Tom Thumb performed here and Frederick Douglass spoke. It was condemned and nearly demolished in the 1970s.

locations.name: Pelham Bay Park
locations.query: Pelham Bay Park, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: At more than 2,700 acres it is over three times the size of Central Park, making it the largest park in the city. It contains salt marsh, forest, a golf course and a lagoon.

locations.name: Nom Wah Tea Parlor
locations.query: Nom Wah Tea Parlor, New York
locations.factShort: Open on the bend of Doyers Street since 1920, which makes it the oldest dim sum parlour in the city. The street's sharp angle was notorious enough in the tong wars to be called the Bloody Angle.

locations.name: The Staten Island Ferry
locations.factShort: Around twenty million passengers a year ride it for nothing, past the Statue of Liberty in both directions. It has run continuously since 1817, first under Cornelius Vanderbilt.

locations.name: Trinity Church
locations.factShort: When it was finished in 1846 its 281-foot spire was the tallest structure in the United States, and it stayed the tallest in New York for over forty years. Alexander Hamilton is buried in the churchyard.

locations.name: Litchfield Villa
locations.factShort: An Italianate mansion built in 1857 for a railroad magnate whose estate the city then bought to make Prospect Park around it. It has housed the Brooklyn parks offices since 1883.

locations.name: Calvary Cemetery
locations.factShort: Around three million people are buried here, more than in any other cemetery in the United States. Its headstones with the Manhattan skyline behind them are one of the most recognisable views in Queens.

locations.name: Loew's Paradise Theater
locations.factShort: One of the five Loew's Wonder Theatres, opened in 1929 with a ceiling painted as a night sky where projected clouds drifted across and stars twinkled overhead. It seated nearly four thousand people on the Grand Concourse.

locations.name: Ellis Island
locations.factShort: Twelve million people were processed through it between 1892 and 1954, and roughly forty percent of Americans have an ancestor who passed through. Only about two percent were ever turned away.

locations.name: Domino Park
locations.factShort: Built on the site of the Domino Sugar refinery, which processed more than half the sugar consumed in the United States at its peak. Salvaged syrup tanks and crane tracks were kept as structure rather than ornament.

locations.name: Bohemian Hall and Beer Garden
locations.factShort: Opened by a Czech and Slovak benevolent society in 1910 and still owned by it, making it the oldest surviving beer garden in New York. Prohibition turned it briefly into a soda garden.

locations.name: Federal Hall
locations.query: Federal Hall National Memorial, New York
locations.factShort: Washington was sworn in as president on a balcony here in 1789, and the Bill of Rights was drafted in the building that stood on the spot. That structure was demolished in 1812; the present Greek Revival customs house replaced it.

locations.name: Soundview Park
locations.factShort: Built on a filled-in salt marsh where the Bronx River meets the East River, with oyster reefs now being seeded off its shore. Its amphitheatre hosts free opera in the summer.

locations.name: Little Island
locations.factShort: An artificial park on 132 concrete tulip-shaped piles in the Hudson, built where Pier 54 stood — the pier where the Carpathia landed Titanic survivors. Its hills were shaped to hide the city from certain angles.

locations.name: The Bushwick Collective
locations.factShort: A few blocks of warehouse walls turned into an open-air mural gallery, started in 2011 by a local man after his mother died. Artists are invited from around the world and the work is repainted continually.

locations.name: Flushing Main Street
locations.factShort: Flushing's Main Street is the heart of one of the largest Chinese communities outside Asia and among the busiest bus corridors in the country. Its subway terminus is the eastern end of the 7 line.

locations.name: The Tenement Museum
locations.factShort: The building at 97 Orchard Street housed around seven thousand people from over twenty countries before its landlord sealed the upper floors in 1935 rather than meet new fire codes. They stayed shut for fifty years and were found essentially intact.

locations.name: Great Kills Park
locations.query: Great Kills Park, Staten Island, New York
locations.factShort: A peninsula built largely from landfill in the 1940s, now part of a national recreation area with a marina and salt marsh. Parts remain fenced off after radium was found in the soil.

locations.name: The Whitney Museum
locations.query: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
locations.factShort: Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney founded it after the Met refused her gift of five hundred works by living American artists. It has moved four times and landed at the foot of the High Line in 2015.

locations.name: Junior's
locations.factShort: Opened on Flatbush Avenue in 1950 and known almost entirely for one thing, a cheesecake with a sponge base rather than a crust. A 1981 fire gutted it and it reopened within the year.

locations.name: Gramercy Park
locations.factShort: The only private park in Manhattan, opened in 1831 and still accessible solely to keyholders in the surrounding buildings. There are said to be fewer than four hundred keys, and they are changed every year.

locations.name: The Throgs Neck Bridge
locations.factShort: Robert Moses built it in 1961 to relieve the Bronx-Whitestone a mile west, and it was among the last of his great river crossings. Its towers rise 360 feet over the entrance to Long Island Sound.

locations.name: Sheepshead Bay
locations.factShort: Named for a fish that has largely vanished from local waters, it kept a working fishing fleet long after the rest of the city's disappeared. The wooden Ocean Avenue footbridge across the bay dates to 1880.

locations.name: The Brooklyn Public Library
locations.factShort: Its facade is shaped like an open book facing Grand Army Plaza, with gilded figures from American literature down the entrance pylons. Begun in 1912, it was interrupted by two wars and not finished until 1941.

locations.name: The United Nations Headquarters
locations.factShort: The eighteen acres it sits on are international territory, with their own postage stamps and fire brigade. Rockefeller bought the land, a stretch of slaughterhouses, and gave it to the UN to keep the organisation in New York.

locations.name: Terrace on the Park
locations.query: Terrace on the Park, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: Built as the heliport for the 1964 World's Fair, lifting visitors in by helicopter from Manhattan rooftops. Its 120-foot pavilion is now a catering hall.

locations.name: Riverside Church
locations.factShort: Its 392-foot tower is the tallest church tower in the United States and holds the largest tuned carillon in the world, seventy-four bells including one of over twenty tons. Martin Luther King gave his Beyond Vietnam speech from its pulpit.

locations.name: The Staten Island Greenbelt
locations.factShort: Nearly 2,800 acres of forest and wetland saved when residents defeated a Robert Moses expressway that would have cut straight through it. Thirty-five miles of trail run through the middle of the borough.

locations.name: The South Street Seaport
locations.factShort: Its cobbled blocks are among the largest concentrations of early nineteenth-century commercial buildings left in Manhattan, saved by a museum that bought them piecemeal in the 1960s. The masts belong to ships the museum keeps in the water.

locations.name: The Prospect Park Zoo
locations.query: Prospect Park Zoo, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Built by the WPA in 1935 with a brick rotunda and animal reliefs over its doors, it was closed in 1988 and rebuilt entirely around smaller species. A sea lion pool sits where the elephant house used to be.

locations.name: Douglaston
locations.factShort: A peninsula of clapboard houses on Little Neck Bay that reads as a New England village and was a private summer colony until the 1920s. The Long Island Rail Road station is its centre.

locations.name: Low Memorial Library
locations.factShort: Its dome is among the largest granite domes in the country, and it was built on the site of the Bloomingdale Insane Asylum. It stopped being a working library in 1934 and now holds offices.

locations.name: The Bronx-Whitestone Bridge
locations.factShort: Opened days before the 1939 World's Fair, its slender deck flexed alarmingly in wind — the same flaw that destroyed Tacoma Narrows a year later. Stiffening trusses were added, then removed again in 2003 for fibreglass fairings.

locations.name: Chelsea Market
locations.factShort: The Oreo was invented in this building when it was the National Biscuit Company factory. The exposed brick and industrial fittings inside are largely original rather than added for effect.

locations.name: Fulton Ferry Landing
locations.query: Fulton Ferry Landing, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Robert Fulton's steam ferry ran from here in 1814, and the crossing is what made Brooklyn commutable and eventually a city. The Brooklyn Bridge put it out of business within a decade of opening.

locations.name: Corona Plaza
locations.factShort: A street closed to traffic in 2012 and turned into a public plaza that now hosts one of the largest street markets in the city, overwhelmingly Latin American. The 7 train runs directly overhead.

locations.name: The Abyssinian Baptist Church
locations.factShort: Founded in 1808 by Black parishioners who refused segregated seating in a Lower Manhattan church, it moved to Harlem in 1923. Adam Clayton Powell Jr. preached here before becoming New York's first Black congressman.

locations.name: The Staten Island Museum
locations.factShort: Founded in 1881 by local naturalists, it is the last general-interest museum in the city holding art, natural history and local history under one roof. Its cicada collection is among the largest anywhere.

locations.name: The Ed Sullivan Theater
locations.factShort: The Beatles played to seventy-three million American viewers from this stage in February 1964, still one of the largest television audiences ever recorded. It was built in 1927 as a Broadway house.

locations.name: Totonno's
locations.factShort: Opened in 1924 by a man who had worked at Lombardi's, and still baking in the same coal oven, which is why it closes when it runs out of dough. Fire gutted it twice and it reopened both times.

locations.name: Broad Channel
locations.factShort: The only inhabited island in Jamaica Bay, where houses stand on stilts over the water and residents held their land on city leases until the 1980s. Its main street is barely a mile long.

locations.name: The African Burial Ground
locations.query: African Burial Ground National Monument, New York
locations.factShort: Construction crews digging a federal office tower in 1991 found human remains twenty-four feet down, and excavation uncovered over four hundred burials from a cemetery holding perhaps fifteen thousand free and enslaved Africans. Work was halted and the site made a national monument.

locations.name: Concourse Plaza
locations.factShort: Opened in 1923 opposite the new Yankee Stadium, it housed visiting ballplayers, borough presidents and wedding parties for decades. Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig both lived in it during the season.

locations.name: Belvedere Castle
locations.factShort: Calvert Vaux built it in 1869 as a folly with no interior purpose, a viewing platform disguised as a Gothic castle. The National Weather Service has taken Central Park's official readings from it since 1919.

locations.name: Marine Park
locations.factShort: Brooklyn's largest park, most of it a salt marsh that was nearly turned into a deepwater port in the 1920s. Its grasslands hold species found almost nowhere else in the city.

locations.name: Rufus King Park
locations.factShort: Eleven acres of what was Rufus King's farm, kept as a park in the middle of downtown Jamaica when the rest was built over. Its oaks predate the American Revolution.

locations.name: Jefferson Market Library
locations.factShort: Built as a courthouse in 1877 and voted one of the ten most beautiful buildings in America at the time, it was slated for demolition in the 1950s. Villagers led by e. e. cummings fought to save it and it became a library in 1967.

locations.name: Ferry Point Park
locations.query: Ferry Point Park, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: A former landfill under the Whitestone Bridge, capped and turned into a public golf course that took nearly twenty years and hundreds of millions of dollars to finish. The salt marsh along its edge was restored at the same time.

locations.name: Strawberry Fields
locations.factShort: Yoko Ono paid for the memorial garden opposite the Dakota, where John Lennon was shot in 1980. The Imagine mosaic was a gift from the city of Naples.

locations.name: The Beard Street Warehouses
locations.factShort: Brick Civil War-era stores built for the Erie Basin, among the oldest surviving warehouse buildings on the New York waterfront. Barges still tie up outside them.

locations.name: Oakland Lake
locations.factShort: A glacial kettle pond left by the retreating ice sheet, one of very few natural bodies of fresh water left in the city. It supplied Bayside's drinking water into the twentieth century.

locations.name: Minton's Playhouse
locations.factShort: Bebop was largely worked out in this room during after-hours sessions in the early 1940s, with Thelonious Monk as house pianist and Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie sitting in. Musicians played fast and in difficult keys partly to keep amateurs off the stand.

locations.name: The Bronx County Courthouse
locations.factShort: A limestone block of a building finished in 1934, ringed by sculpted friezes and freestanding figures by nine different artists working on a New Deal commission. It sits at the highest point of the Grand Concourse.

locations.name: Fort Tryon Park
locations.factShort: Rockefeller bought the estate, had Olmsted's son landscape it and gave it to the city in 1935. It was the site of the last stand at Fort Washington in 1776, defended in part by Margaret Corbin after her husband was killed at his gun.

locations.name: Vinegar Hill
locations.factShort: A few surviving blocks of Belgian block and Greek Revival houses beside the Navy Yard, named after a battle in the 1798 Irish rebellion to attract Irish buyers. Most of the neighbourhood was demolished for power plants and housing.

locations.name: Aqueduct Racetrack
locations.factShort: Named for the Brooklyn water conduit that ran beside the original 1894 course, it is the only thoroughbred track within New York City limits. Winter racing here continues in weather that closes most other tracks.

locations.name: Stone Street
locations.factShort: One of the first paved streets in New Amsterdam, cobbled in 1658 reportedly after a brewer's wife complained about the mud. The buildings on it now date mostly from after the 1835 fire.

locations.name: Spuyten Duyvil
locations.factShort: The name is Dutch, roughly spouting devil, for the treacherous tidal currents where the Harlem River meets the Hudson. The channel was straightened in 1895, cutting Marble Hill off from Manhattan and leaving it physically attached to the Bronx.

locations.name: The Conservatory Garden
locations.factShort: Central Park's only formal garden, built in 1937 where a glass conservatory had stood since the 1890s. It is divided into Italian, French and English sections and is the park's designated quiet zone.

locations.name: Restoration Plaza
locations.factShort: Robert Kennedy walked the neighbourhood in 1966 and helped found what became the country's first community development corporation, housed in a converted milk bottling plant. It is still operating.

locations.name: Woodside
locations.factShort: Long the heart of Irish Queens, and still holding some of the oldest pubs in the borough, though it is now equally Filipino and Latin American. Its station is one of the few where the 7 train meets the Long Island Rail Road.

locations.name: The New York Marble Cemetery
locations.query: New York Marble Cemetery, New York
locations.factShort: The city's first non-sectarian burial ground, opened in 1830 with 156 underground marble vaults and no headstones at all — names are cut into the wall instead. It is hidden mid-block and open only a few days a year.

locations.name: Co-op City
locations.factShort: Fifteen thousand apartments across three hundred acres, the largest housing cooperative in the world, built on the site of a failed amusement park called Freedomland. Around forty thousand people live in it.

locations.name: Governors Island
locations.factShort: An army post for nearly two centuries and a Coast Guard base after that, sold to the people of New York in 2003 for one dollar. Its southern half is landfill from digging the Lexington Avenue subway.

locations.name: Di Fara Pizza
locations.query: Di Fara Pizza, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: Domenico De Marco made every pie himself from 1965 until shortly before his death in 2022, which is why the queues ran for hours. He snipped basil over each one with scissors.

locations.name: The Newtown Creek Nature Walk
locations.factShort: A landscaped path beside one of the most polluted waterways in America, alongside a sewage plant whose digester eggs are lit blue at night. Beneath the creek lies an oil spill larger than the Exxon Valdez.

locations.name: Fraunces Tavern
locations.factShort: Washington said farewell to his officers in the Long Room here in December 1783, weeping as he embraced them. Its proprietor Samuel Fraunces, a man of colour from the West Indies, later ran the presidential household.

locations.name: The Staten Island Zoo
locations.factShort: Opened in 1936 as the country's first zoo built specifically for education rather than display, on eight acres. Its rattlesnake collection was for years the most complete anywhere.

locations.name: New York City Hall
locations.query: New York City Hall, New York
locations.factShort: The oldest city hall in America still used for its original purpose, finished in 1812. Its back was faced in cheap brownstone rather than marble because the city assumed nobody would ever build north of it.

locations.name: The City Reliquary
locations.factShort: A museum of New York ephemera that began in a ground-floor apartment window, showing subway tokens, seltzer bottles and paint chips from the Statue of Liberty. It became a proper storefront museum in 2006.

locations.name: Gould Memorial Library
locations.query: Gould Memorial Library, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: Stanford White modelled it on the Pantheon, with a coffered dome and green marble columns, for what was then NYU's uptown campus. It sits directly behind the Hall of Fame colonnade.

locations.name: Old St. Patrick's Cathedral
locations.factShort: The city's original Catholic cathedral, finished in 1815 and ringed by a brick wall its parishioners once defended with muskets against anti-Catholic mobs. Its catacombs still hold burials.

locations.name: The Ear Inn
locations.factShort: The house was built around 1770 for an aide of Washington's and stood on the shoreline before landfill pushed the Hudson back. The bar's neon B was painted over to read EAR so it would not need landmark approval for a new sign.

locations.name: Bowling Green
locations.factShort: The oldest public park in the city, leased in 1733 for one peppercorn a year. A mob pulled down a statue of George III here in 1776 and melted it into musket balls.

locations.name: Plumb Beach
locations.factShort: One of the last horseshoe crab spawning beaches in the city, where thousands come ashore each spring on the high tides around the full moon. It is reachable only from the Belt Parkway.

locations.name: Queensbridge Park
locations.factShort: It sits beside Queensbridge Houses, the largest public housing development in North America, and under the Queensboro Bridge. Nas, Mobb Deep and MC Shan all came out of the blocks around it.

locations.name: The Schomburg Center
locations.query: Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, New York
locations.factShort: Built around the private collection of Arturo Schomburg, a Puerto Rican of African descent told as a schoolboy that Black people had no history. He is buried nearby and his ashes are interred in the centre's floor.

locations.name: The Longwood Historic District
locations.query: Longwood Historic District, Bronx, New York
locations.factShort: Rows of near-identical speculative houses built between 1897 and 1901 for workers arriving with the new subway. Their intact stoops and bays make it one of the best-preserved streetscapes in the borough.

locations.name: The Astor Place Cube
locations.factShort: An eight-foot steel cube on a hidden post that any two people can spin by pushing a corner, installed in 1967 as temporary public art and never removed. Students once found a live chicken sealed inside it.

locations.name: The Williamsburgh Savings Bank Tower
locations.factShort: Brooklyn's tallest building for over eighty years, with the largest four-faced clock in the United States at its top. Its banking hall ceiling is a mosaic vault, and the tower was converted to flats in 2007.

locations.name: The Wyckoff-Bennett Homestead
locations.factShort: A Dutch farmhouse of about 1766 still in private hands, with the names of Hessian officers quartered there during the Revolution scratched into a windowpane. It is one of the few colonial houses in the city never opened as a museum.

locations.name: Bowne Park
locations.factShort: Twelve acres that were the estate of Walter Bowne, a mayor of New York in the 1830s, bought by the city in 1925. Its pond is a remnant of the ice pond that served the estate.

locations.name: Stuyvesant Town
locations.factShort: Built for returning veterans on eighteen blocks of demolished tenements, and openly refused to rent to Black tenants until a decade-long legal fight forced it to change in 1950. It holds over eleven thousand apartments.

locations.name: The Waldorf Astoria
locations.query: Waldorf Astoria New York, New York
locations.factShort: The original stood where the Empire State Building now does; the hotel moved to Park Avenue in 1931 and became the largest in the world. It has a private railway platform beneath it that Franklin Roosevelt used.

locations.name: Coney Island Creek Park
locations.query: Coney Island Creek Park, Brooklyn, New York
locations.factShort: A half-sunk yellow submarine sits in the mud here, built in the 1960s by a shipyard worker hoping to salvage treasure and never finished. Coney Island was a genuine island until the creek was partly filled.

locations.name: Creedmoor
locations.query: Creedmoor Psychiatric Center, Queens, New York
locations.factShort: The site was a rifle range where the National Rifle Association held its first matches in the 1870s before becoming a psychiatric hospital. At its peak in the 1950s it held around seven thousand patients.

locations.name: Grace Church
locations.factShort: James Renwick was twenty-three when he designed it, and it made his name well before St. Patrick's. Broadway bends around it because the farmer who owned the land refused to sell a straight route through.

locations.name: Postcards
locations.factShort: Two white wing-like forms framing the gap in the skyline where the towers stood, holding profiles of the 274 Staten Islanders who died. They are angled so the sun aligns with the site each September 11.

locations.name: Tudor City
locations.factShort: The first residential skyscraper complex in the world, built in 1927 on a bluff above slaughterhouses — which is why its big apartments face away from the river. The land below is now the United Nations.

locations.name: The Old Stone House
locations.factShort: Four hundred Maryland troops held this farmhouse against overwhelming British numbers in August 1776, buying time for Washington's army to escape across the East River. The building was reconstructed in 1934 from its own excavated stones.

locations.name: Elmhurst
locations.factShort: Founded by the Dutch in 1652 as Middleburgh and renamed Newtown by the English, it is now among the most ethnically diverse neighbourhoods on earth. St. James Church, built in 1734, still stands on Broadway.

locations.name: The Seagram Building
locations.factShort: Mies van der Rohe set it back ninety feet from Park Avenue to create a public plaza, an unheard-of surrender of buildable land that later zoning turned into a citywide incentive. Its bronze skin was left to weather without polishing.

locations.name: The Smallpox Hospital
locations.factShort: A Gothic Revival hospital of 1856 built to isolate smallpox patients on what was then Blackwell's Island, abandoned in the 1950s and left to collapse. It is the only ruin with landmark status in New York City.
